body: Most AI work is priced in one of four ways, and some firms don’t publish a price at all. None of these is wrong. Each one puts a different part of the risk on you, so it helps to know which part before you sign.
## How AI work is charged

Here is a published example of each, with what to watch. These are examples of how AI is priced, not attacks on these companies. Some of these tools are the right choice for a partner, and our AI assistant rollout service sets them up.
[table]
## Six questions to ask before you sign
Whichever way a firm charges, these questions show whether you can check the price.
[questions]
[pull quote] “Honest prices, published up front.” Alliance AI Partners · the line on our pricing page
## Why our prices can be lower
Two things let Alliance AI Partners charge less than most AI firms.
AI does the repetitive work. First drafts, testing, content production and data entry take fewer hours, so a project needs fewer billable hours.
We’re based in the Philippines. Our costs are lower than those of firms in the US, the UK or Australia, and we pass the difference on to you.
Lower cost doesn’t mean less care. AI takes over the repetitive hours, and a person still reviews every piece of work before it reaches you.
## What we do instead
Our honest pricing promise is a list you can check:
[promise]

If you’re comparing us with another firm, ask us the same six questions, then compare the answers. Our usual first project is the AI check-up: in [two weeks], we find where AI could save you time or money, and you get a fixed quote for the first fix.
[link] See what the AI check-up includes → /ai-check-up
## Sources

rows: Most US and Australian web development agencies on Clutch charge US$100 to US$149 an hour. [key 1]
Slow work costs more, and the final bill is hard to predict.
Microsoft 365 Copilot is US$30 per user a month, paid yearly, on top of a Microsoft 365 plan. For 50 people, that’s US$1,500 a month. [key 2]
Costs rise with every person you add.
Intercom’s Fin is US$0.99 per outcome, with seats extra. Smith.ai’s AI receptionist is US$150 a month for 75 calls, then US$2.50 a call. [keys 3, 4]
Busy months cost more, so budgets are hard to set.
SEO retainers on Clutch run from US$2,000 to US$20,000 a month, averaging US$3,199. [key 5]
It isn’t always clear what the retainer buys.
Some firms share prices only after a sales call.
You can’t compare until you’ve given up an hour.

items.title: Is there a published starting price?
items.text: A starting price lets you compare firms before anyone books a call.

items.title: Is the quote fixed, and does it list everything?
items.text: A fixed quote names every charge. Any change should be quoted before the work is done.

items.title: Does the price grow with every seat?
items.text: Per-seat fees rise each time you add a person, even when the work stays the same.

items.title: How is AI usage billed?
items.text: Model fees are a real cost. Ask whether they’re passed on at cost and shown on the invoice.

items.title: Can you cancel a monthly plan?
items.text: Ask how much notice you need to give, and what you keep when you leave.

items.title: Who owns what is built?
items.text: You should own the code, the data and the documents, even if you stop working together.

promise: Published starting prices for every core service.
A fixed quote before work starts that lists everything we’ll charge. Changes are quoted before we do them.
No per-seat fees on the tools we build.
AI usage, like model fees, passed on at cost and shown on the invoice.
Monthly plans you can cancel with [30] days’ notice.
If an off-the-shelf tool or a simpler fix costs you less, we say so.

notes: A sample, marked twice: the Info Alert under the meta, and ‘Sample article’ on every related card. Every word comes from the Brand DNA: the ‘How other AI firms charge’ table (examples and what to watch, with its fairness line that these are examples, not attacks), the price rules, ‘Why we cost less’, the honest pricing promise and the buyer answer that a person reviews every piece of work. The table drops the Brand DNA’s fourth column (‘What we do instead’) because the promise list below says it in checkable form, and so the bracketed, unconfirmed ‘[A flat monthly price, with AI usage passed on at cost]’ is not published. Every figure sits in the article body section, with a Source key on the table cell and a dated line in the source list (Clutch September 2026, Microsoft, Intercom, Smith.ai; retrieved 2026-11-02); the US$1,500 for 50 seats is our sum of the Microsoft price. Read time 3 min, from the 675 words in the standfirst and body. Placeholders kept: [Name], [Role], [Publish date], [30], [two weeks], [once a month]. One Primary (Subscribe in the newsletter strip); the AI check-up is offered by an underlined link at the end of the article and by the header’s Secondary. The ribbon appears twice: the rule over the pull quote and the rule along the newsletter card. The pull quote is our own tagline (‘Honest prices, published up front.’, Brand DNA section 7) with an attribution that names Alliance AI Partners. Owner check before publishing: the article names other firms’ prices, and the Brand DNA says to check anything public that names one; re-check each price on the day it goes live.
